Author: @koelhomem
Content: Francesinha... all wrong, man. The sauce should be like a thick sauce... Not purée. What you called chourico, it's not chourico. In fact, chourico has no part in francesinha... EVER! We use something called "linguica", a type of portuguese fresh sausage. The layers should be composed as it follows: slice of bread (normal or toasted... your choice), slice of ham, steak, cheese, slice of bread, ham, luinguica, cheese, slice of bread. You put the fried egg ON TOP of the finished thing and THEN you cover everything with slices of cheese (I mean, really everything). Even the egg. Then you pour the francesinha sauce all over the francesinha. The hot sauce will melt the cheese and form the pool around it. You can add more sauce later on. THEN, you also serve french fries with it. All around the francesinha. And francesinha IT'S NOT a national dish. It is, yes, a traditional dish in Porto (Northern Portugal), my hometown and place of birth. Take this as a criticism, yes. You're giving people a misconception of everything the francesinha is.

Author: @cs256
Content:
Guga, I’ve got to be honest—I'm a bit disappointed with your Greek sandwich. That’s actually my favourite, and it's called pitta me souvlaki. A few key points were off.

First, the meat must be grilled on skewers—true souvlaki style. Once it's cooked, you need to give it a proper bath in a mix of lemon juice, olive oil, and oregano. Only after the bath should you season it with salt, pepper, and yes, more oregano—but never grill it with oregano on, as it burns.

You also forgot the essential sauce—tzatziki! And don’t skip the fresh tomato slices, thinly cut red onion mixed with parsley, and of course, fries (patates tiganites) sprinkled with paprika and a little more salt. Wrap all that in warm pitta and you’ve got the real deal.

Happy to answer any questions if you'd like more Greek tips!

Today we explored sandwich classics from around the world, and one of the standouts comes from the Netherlands: the "broodje warm vlees", or Dutch warm meat sandwich. This traditional Dutch favorite is a beloved comfort food and typically includes:
 Warm sliced meat – usually pork roast or fricandeau (a Dutch-style lean roast), served warm and tender.
 Peanut satay sauce – a rich, creamy sauce with Indonesian roots, often slightly spicy, generously poured over the meat.
 Crispy fried onions – adding a satisfying crunch and savory punch.
It’s a classic you’ll find in Dutch lunchrooms, cafés, and even at gas stations — simple, messy, and seriously tasty. Definitely one of the Netherlands' coziest food traditions.

Author: @Tonalmitzin
Content:
Fun fact: apart from the Cuban Sandwich, in México we also have something called "torta cubana", which is a telera (like a baggette bread) with pretty much everything at hand: fried ham,  pork leg, quesillo (a type of cheese from Oaxaca), sausages, chorizo, avocado, refried beans, jalapeño peppers or chipotle, onion, red tomato, mayonaise, mustard and whatever the food place add on.

Not to say that it is the best torta (sandwich) in México, but it shares the "cuban" name on it, although it is not from Cuba either.

Try the cemitas (from Puebla), torta de chilaquiles (from Mexico City), torta de cochinita pibil (from Yucatán) or torta de carnitas (from Michoacán) next time. They're the best sandwiches from México.

Author: @RaspK
Content:
10:30 Oh man... The other Greeks in the comments... [yikes]

Whoever responded to you messed up. Gyro (from Greek γύρος < γύρω [around; in this context, from being on a rotisserie spit, derived from döner, frankly]) refers only to the sliced-meat food item, and if it has extended to all other versions... it's the same as with bologna referring to low-quality sausage, rather than the original mortadella di Bologna as it does in Italy.

What you have here is called σουβλάκι ("skewer" - the word σούβλα meaning "spit"), and specifically the version that's wrapped as a sandwich (of note: people in Salonica specifically mean *this* when they ask for a σάντουιτς). It's also eaten as is, but has dropped in favour with people over the wrap version. Not using tzatziki is also normal, because *_in the past_* they wouldn't. It became the norm fairly recently, i.e. in living memory. In various places, it's still not the norm (e.g. in Crete, it's often made with Greek yogurt).

Content:
I understand why you made the Greek "wrapped souvlaki" COMPLETELY WRONG, since HERE (in Greece) they make it wrong too!!!

The GENUINE TRADITIONAL one is made with the following ingredients:

- pork skewer (from loin & neck) - "gyros" is the newer version, "stolen" from the Turkish "döner"
- chopped fresh tomato (and NOT large pieces or tomato paste either)
- chopped onion WITH ABSOLUTELLY parsley
- Paprika
- Red pepper
- Salt
- YOGURT (if you want it most traditional) or at least "Tzatziki", but in SMALL amount so that the "pita" pie doesn't get "soaked"

...and ABSOLUTELY NOTHING ELSE inside!!!
Whatever else you want to eat with it (like fries potatos), you placing them NEXT in a different plate.

Content: Guga , the greek traditional pitta sandwich is made in different way ! Recipe : Pitta bread finished on charcoal grill or on hot surface plate with a little olive oil and a  little bit of salt and oregano. It has no connection with turkish kebab .  As you should know in Hellas ( Greece for barbarians ) started everything good even the food . We the Greeks were always cosmopolitans (greek word for "the citizens of cosmos - world)  and we learn and use things from  everywhere ( like tomatoes and potatoes from America) but we always do things in our way we don't have to copy. The saddest thing about people visiting "Greece" is that very few have the opportunity to taste real food and experience the greek way. That's tourism , not the real thing. I hope you make better research about foreign cuisine. Keep  working hard , best of regards!

Author: @richardelliott8917
Content:
Guga,you didn't even mention let alone do is the one sandwich that is sold to the millions of Aussies every day.
The Australian steak sandwich.
You will need a good piece of skirt,rump or porterhouse steak. It doesn't have to be thick as otherwise it will take too long. Season your steak with salt, pepper and a slight rub with Worchester sauce. While letting it rest for a couple of minutes,fry your sliced onion in butter and season with salt and freshly ground pepper. After the first onion stir,place your steak on top of the onion and cover for a minute, remove, place steak on a hot grill onion side down first. This allows you to cook without burning the onion vapour/caramelizing straight away and getting a sour/slight burn flavour. After you get a caramelization on both sides of steak,rest/slow steam the steak on the finishing fried onions. Serve between two slices of bread,a lettuce leaf, sliced tomato, cheese and a slice of Beetroot. Goes great with a nice tasting COLD beer. Great show,love watching what you are doing with the experiments. Don't stop what you do. Great job👍
From a brother down under 🤔

Content: You missed South Africa. Known for 1 very Iconic sandwich, namely the Braaibroodjie: A normal toasted sandwich with butter, tomato, finely sliced onion and cheddar cheese. What makes it iconic for SA is that it's toasted over an open fire grill or on coal grill. You could toast it over briquettes or a charcoal grill as well. To grill it without burning it, you turn the bread really really fast, like once every 10 seconds. This allows the butter to grill through the bread slices, giving it a nice yellow glow at the end, which is what you want for an Amazing taste.

Tirosalata

Ugareza

Content: Missed out on a couple of key elements to the Choripán. First and foremost - and this was a big surprise coming from you - GRILL YOUR BREAD! Huge flavor and texture difference. And finally, the chimichurri is only half the condiments. The other should be a salsa criolla - diced tomato’s and white onions tossed with olive oil, lemon juice, and red wine vinegar. Or at the very least some diced onions with the olive oil, lemon juice, and red wine vinegar. That sharp onion bite and extra acidity counteracts with that savory and earthy chorizo rich with olive oil, and the fattiness of the chorizo all on a nice, crispy grilled baguette. Brings that up to A tier, maybe even S tier.

Author: @mehmetturgut6154
Content:
im not gonna fight over who made döner or gyro or shawarma etc. but making german style döner (ground meat, salad,yogurt and other random bs) and calling it turkish aaaaaaand making souvlaki,putting it inside the bread and calling it gyro is diabolical. 

its easy
turkish = loaf of bread or flatbread, chicken or meat döner ( no minced meat ) and sometimes tomatoe and lettuce (no sauce necessary since the döner has layers of animal fat)
greek = same breads but also has pork as an option, lettuce tomatoe tzatiki (ionno how to spell cacık),maybe french fries.(also its ground meat most of the time)
german = pita bread,whole garden of veggies for some reason,meat (which is almost always ground meat).fries, and to mask the flavour put any sauce you can find.
mena region (shawarma) = meat or chicken (usually chicken and no ground meat (chicken thighs)) flatbread,toum (garlic sauce), sometimes pickle and fries aaaaaaaaand za pepsi

TL:DR 
Döner=meat bread 
gyro=usually minced meat,bread,salad,tzatkizikzki
germany ( for some reason )=bread,whole head of lettuce,ground meat, every sauce u can find
shawarma =chicken,bread,garlic sauce,fries, ZA PEPSI

Content:
I'd love to see the opinion on the Aussie classic, the Bunnings Snag (Named as such because you go to the hardware store Bunnings, and they're cooking these for charity, and us Aussies having weird names for things, I have no idea how sausage turned into snag), though it could also be considered a hotdog.

Ingredients:
1 Beef Sausage
1 Handful of sliced onions
1 Slice of white bread
Heinz Ketchup

Preparation:
Cook the Sausage and the Onions on a barbecue
Put the sausage in the bread, diagonally
Add onion on top (Technically health and safety banned this because they were worried about the onions falling off and someone slipping on them, but this is the superior way)
Add the ketchup to taste

And thats the Bunnings Snag.

Content:
Guga, I grew up in and around Philadelphia. I almost shut off when your cheesesteak had mayo, and then definitely shut it off at Swiss cheese. I don’t think you have ever been to Philadelphia. 

Mayo on a cheesesteak is a bigger no-no than green peppers. Not authentic!! It will get you punched on some streets there, unless it’s a cheesesteak hoagie. Swiss cheese will get you accused of being John Kerry. He got ridiculed for requesting Swiss in 2004.

The most common cheeses are Cooper Sharp American, Provolone, and a Cheez Wiz variant.

A pizza steak will usually have mozzarella and/or provolone with marinara.

The underrated (and better) philly sandwich is the roast pork italian.

Author: @KostasHolopain
Content:
Guga, I'm sorry man, this was not Gyro, although it looked tasty!
Gyro is made the same way as Dönner, but with pork meat and different spices, although chicken is also common nowadays. Not when I was a kid though... half a century ago! 
Dönner can be found also, usually made from Beef, although the traditional recipe calls for 50% beef and 50% Lamb.
As for the fillings, these vary regionally, but in the mainland Greece, the traditional filling is sliced Tomato, Tzatziki, sliced onions, Parsley, sweet Paprika and red Pepper .
A modern adition is fries.
In Northern Greece however, Lettuce, Mustard spicy cheese cream are common.
Both taste fantastic and regionally, you can find variations in meat, but they are not called Gyro- including spicy meatballs, bifteki and various saucages.
Source: I'm a native and have eaten the stuff in most of the big cities and islands... and in dosens of villages. For a long period, it was everyday food for me, due to working  in walking distance of at least 10 different establishments that served their own variations.

Content: 2:05 Guga! I love you, but maaaan, you did a huge disservice to the Torta Ahogada. As a Mexican born and raised in Guadalajara (where torta ahogada was born) I can guarantee that if done right, it’ll absolutely deserve an S-tier spot! There’s a huge room for improvement on your take, but mostly, it’s the bread. The correct type is called Birote Salado which is a special kind of birote (similar to german Brötchen, but way crunchier) that keeps the torta mostly unaffected from drenching it in salsa. Speaking of which, tomato salsa is meant to be less thicker and non-spicy, but a second hot chile de árbol salsa can (must) be added to your preference. Avocado is ok, but not a very common ingredient tbh. One key ingredient missing tho, is lime juice, which is added on top of everything. And last but definitely not least, PLEASE drop the cotija cheese and cilantro, those are just plain wrong. I strongly recommend you go watch Mark Wiens’s street food vlog in Guadalajara from a month ago, where he visited three of the top torta ahogada shops in the city, each of them with their own unique recipe. I really hope you can give it a second chance. It’s a life changing sandwich I tell ya!

Author: @NULUSIOS
Content:
That's not Greek souvlaki. I request a rematch.

Find REAL Greek souvlaki (which apparently is not easy in the States):
- Greek pita (salted/unsalted, with some olive oil or not)
- Real skewer pork meat (this didn't look like it at all and some fat is a must in it) or gyros (not doner, that is a different mixture) or "bifteki" (minced meat with some herbs and extras).
- Red pepper
- Tzatziki (some put plain yogurt, but this is the real thing)
- Tomato
- Onions
- Some make some a red sauce (sometimes hot), esp. for the bifteki option.
- Fries (some put an overwhelming amount, but this is mostly to "cover" for other... issues, like amount of meat)

...not the other cr*p you added in your version.

...everything is optional but I suggest you only remove the potatoes to appreciate the rest of it (because potatoes tend to fill you) and maybe the sauce if you cannot find original (which is always hand made).

Yes they do make many variations (like putting different sauce), but the one you shown is NOT even close to a popular one.

I understand you want to make content, but please try to be true.

Author: @714milky
Content:
I cried a bit....that is NOT how you make a torta Ahogada 😢. 

First of all, you need bread thats a few days old. That way it's crispy and can hold up to beign "drowned" in the salsa. Otherwise u end up with a soggy mess. 

Secondly, avocado doesn't belong....just because its a torta doesn't mean it nees avocado!

The sauce is all wrong. It's supposed to have a tomato-based non-spicy sauce as the first layer, then it's to be topped off with a pure chile de arbol salsa that is extremely spicy. Those two in combination make the traditional torta ahogada sauce. Depending on the level of spicy you want, you can ask for it. Non-spicy, just the base tomato. half drowned with a ladle of the super spicy sauce over top. Or full drowned where the entire sandwich is dipped in the spicy sauce and is incredibly hot. 

And lastly, there is absolutely zero need for Cotija cheese on the sandwich. I think it was more of a garnish in this case. But there is no torta ahogada that needs cheese. 

This is a very traditional and important sandwich for the State of Jalisco, specifically Guadalajara. So get it right Guga!

Im a big fan btw not hating. But informing!
